content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching the lion is most commonly a symbol of royal, sovereign power and majesty, applied above all to Jesus Christ as the 'Lion of the tribe of Judah'—the conquering messianic King descended from Judah and David. The image conveys kingship, strength, courage, and victorious authority.", "primary_basis": ["Revelation 5:5 (Christ as 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David' who has conquered)", "Genesis 49:9-10 (Jacob's blessing: 'Judah is a lion's cub... the scepter shall not depart from Judah')", "Hosea 11:10 (the LORD roaring like a lion as His people return)", "Numbers 23:24; 24:9 (Israel rising up like a lion in Balaam's oracles)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Satan or the demonic adversary as a devouring, predatory threat—'your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.' This is the standard negative use of the lion image and is taught nearly as often as the Christological use.", "basis": ["1 Peter 5:8", "Psalm 22:13, 21 (lions surrounding and menacing the righteous sufferer, read Christologically of the passion)", "2 Timothy 4:17 ('rescued from the lion's mouth')"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "God Himself as a lion in judgment—Yahweh's fierce, unstoppable wrath against unfaithful Israel or the nations.", "basis": ["Hosea 5:14; 13:7-8", "Amos 1:2; 3:8 ('The lion has roared; who will not fear?')", "Jeremiah 25:38; 49:19", "Lamentations 3:10", "Isaiah 31:4"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Hostile earthly kingdoms, kings, or oppressive enemies of God's people (e.g., Babylon; Nebuchadnezzar's lion-beast in Daniel's vision; wicked rulers).", "basis": ["Daniel 7:4 (the first beast 'like a lion')", "Jeremiah 4:7; 50:17", "Proverbs 28:15 (a wicked ruler like a roaring lion)", "Nahum 2:11-13 (Nineveh as a lions' den)", "Ezekiel 19:1-9 (princes of Israel as lions)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Generic emblem of strength, courage, and boldness of the righteous ('the righteous are bold as a lion'), used in moral and devotional teaching without specific referent.", "basis": ["Proverbs 28:1", "Proverbs 30:30", "2 Samuel 17:10; 1 Chronicles 12:8"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Eschatological peace imagery: the lion lying down with (or dwelling alongside) the lamb/calf as a symbol of the messianic age's restoration of creation.", "basis": ["Isaiah 11:6-7", "Isaiah 65:25"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "In the traditional four-living-creatures scheme, the lion as the emblem of Mark the Evangelist (patristic and iconographic tradition following Irenaeus, Jerome, and Augustine, with varying assignments).", "basis": ["Revelation 4:7", "Ezekiel 1:10; 10:14"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Deliverance/vindication motif: God shutting the lions' mouths as a type of rescue of the faithful and, in some patristic readings, a type of Christ's resurrection from the pit.", "basis": ["Daniel 6:16-23", "Hebrews 11:33", "Psalm 91:13"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "The lion is a well-recognized but deliberately bivalent biblical symbol: interpreters across traditions (patristic, medieval bestiary, Reformation, and modern evangelical/academic) uniformly note that context determines whether it signifies Christ/God in regal power or Satan/enemies in devouring menace. The Christological 'Lion of Judah' reading is the most frequently cited primary meaning in Christian teaching (reinforced culturally by C.S. Lewis's Aslan), with 1 Peter 5:8's satanic lion as the standard counterpoint. Because the symbol is context-dependent rather than univocal, the consensus is on this dual/polyvalent framework rather than on a single fixed referent."}
